name: Hydroxyzine

lead: Hydroxyzine is an older prescription antihistamine, approved by the FDA in 1956, used for anxiety and tension, allergic itching and sedation around surgery. Looksmaxxing users discuss it for its sedating and anti-itch effects, tying better sleep to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.
It blocks histamine H1 receptors and, because it enters the brain, causes sedation. It is studied for anxiety disorders and urticaria; no studies look at its effect on appearance.

paras: It is taken by mouth on prescription, often in the evening because of the drowsiness, for anxiety or itch. Sedation is felt within the first hours after a dose.
Drowsiness, dry mouth and dizziness are common. Labels warn about combined sedation with alcohol and other depressants, rare heart rhythm effects and seizures, and use in early pregnancy.

angle.text: Hydroxyzine is a sedating antihistamine used for anxiety, itch and sleep, discussed on the theory that better sleep and calmer skin show up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for anxiety and itch; its effect on looks has not been studied.

lead: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine of the piperazine class that has been in clinical use since the 1950s. It was first made by Union Chimique Belge in 1956 and approved in the US later that year [1][2]. Its US label covers symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension, itching from allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria and atopic or contact dermatitis, and sedation before and after general anaesthesia [1][3].

The wiki lists it in the recovery category because of two practical effects: it makes people drowsy, and it relieves itch. People who use it describe a chain from calmer evenings and easier sleep, to better rest, to better recovery and a more rested appearance, and from itch relief to less scratching and more comfortable skin. Published research addresses anxiety, itch and sedation around surgery rather than appearance outcomes.

Reviews list it among treatments for anxiety disorders and for urticaria [4][5]. Its sedating effect is linked to its ability to cross into the brain, unlike non-sedating antihistamines [6]. In the body it is partly converted to cetirizine, the active metabolite sold separately as a non-sedating antihistamine [2][7]. In 2023 it was among the most commonly prescribed medicines in the US, with more than 15 million prescriptions [2].
infobox: 1956 (made by UCB; US approval later that year) [2]

paras: The US label for hydroxyzine pamoate lists anxiety and tension, allergic pruritus and sedative premedication among its indications [1][3]. A 2020 review of anxiety pharmacotherapy discusses it among approved and off-label options for anxiety disorders [4]. Urticaria reviews describe sedating antihistamines as a long-standing therapy for itch [5].

The label indicates hydroxyzine for pruritus due to allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria, atopic and contact dermatoses, and histamine-mediated itch [3]. Users on a T Nation forum thread about itching that worsened at night describe taking Atarax, the hydrochloride brand, for burning and itching skin [8].

Forum members discuss hydroxyzine as a prescription option for insomnia and anxiety. In a T Nation thread on insomnia, a member plans to ask a doctor about it for sleep, and in a thread on overtraining and insomnia another suggests asking a doctor about a short-term prescription for it or similar medicines [9][10]. Wikipedia reports that a 2023 meta-review found it effective for sleep onset but less so for maintaining sleep through the night, and that a 2022 network meta-analysis found limited evidence for its use in insomnia [2]. A systematic review of its efficacy and safety for sleep in adults was published in 2023 [11].
Other forum members mention using it for situational anxiety, for example before an event they expect to be crowded [12].

The label describes use as a sedative before and after general anaesthesia [3]. Registered trials have examined it as premedication in strabismus surgery and for preventing itch after spinal morphine [13][14]. An open-label case series in interstitial cystitis and a pilot trial with pentosan polysulfate also tested it [15][16].

The label describes side effects as usually mild and transitory. Common effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness and headache; the label and reviews warn of added sedation with alcohol and other central nervous system depressants, and of rare involuntary movements and seizures at high doses [1][3]. The label also lists acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis and fixed drug eruptions in post-marketing reports [3].

Wikipedia notes QT prolongation as a serious effect, that hydroxyzine is on lists of drugs to avoid in older adults, and that long-term use has been linked to tardive dyskinesia [2]. Use is contraindicated in early pregnancy per the label, and the label advises that nursing mothers not receive it [1][3]. Tolerance to its sedative effect is reported to develop within days, which is one reason it is usually prescribed short-term or as needed [2].

Hydroxyzine is a potent histamine H1 receptor inverse agonist; weaker activity at serotonin 5-HT2A, dopamine D2 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors may contribute to its anxiolytic effect [2]. A 2003 study found sedating H1 antagonists such as hydroxyzine are not limited by P-glycoprotein at the blood-brain barrier, unlike non-sedating antihistamines, which fits their central effects [6]. A PET study reported brain H1 receptor occupancy of about 68 percent after a single 30 mg dose, with sleepiness correlating with occupancy [2].

Oral and intramuscular doses are absorbed quickly, with peak concentrations after about two hours. It is metabolised in the liver mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5, and roughly 45 percent becomes cetirizine [2]. Its elimination half-life is about 20 hours in adults, longer in older people and shorter in children [2]. Cetirizine is the carboxylated metabolite with high affinity for H1 receptors [7].

Union Chimique Belge first made hydroxyzine in 1956, and it was approved for sale in the US later that year [2]. It is sold under brands including Atarax for the hydrochloride and Vistaril for the pamoate salt [2]. It is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and Australia [2].

Hydroxyzine is discussed less than other sleep or anxiety options in appearance-focused communities, and the mentions found are in forums about training and insomnia, where members describe it as an antihistamine used for sleep or situational anxiety [9][10][12]. Some members of those forums describe self-managing a wider set of supplements and prescriptions, including hydroxyzine for sleep [17].

Registered trials include a strabismus surgery premedication study, a trial of itch prevention after spinal morphine and a pilot study with opioid withdrawal [13][14][18]. A trial of hydroxyzine for anxiety in people with eating disorders was withdrawn [19]. An open-label case series of 90 respondents among 140 interstitial cystitis patients reported about a 40 percent reduction in symptom scores, rising to 55 percent in those with a history of allergies, and a 2003 pilot trial examined it with pentosan polysulfate [15][16]. A 1975 double-blind crossover study in 23 children with asthma combined theophylline with ephedrine and hydroxyzine [20]. A 1983 trial compared midazolam with hydroxyzine as intramuscular premedication [21]. Wikipedia cites a 2010 Cochrane review finding hydroxyzine better than placebo for generalised anxiety disorder [2]. No studies were found on hydroxyzine for appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: Hydroxyzine appears in forum discussions mainly as a prescription antihistamine for sleep, itch or situational anxiety rather than as an appearance product [9][10].
